extracted.intended_audience: Principal investigators, grant applicants, institutional administrators, and postdocs involved with NIH funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance about how NRSA stipend levels interact with salaries charged to NIH research grants, what is allowable supplementation, tuition coverage for NRSA trainees, and practical budgeting considerations for PIs preparing NIH grant budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: NRSA levels do not dictate institutional or research-grant salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: “The NRSA level for those on fellowships (institutional T32 or individual F32 / F31 awards) does not directly dictate what salary is paid at any particular applicant institution nor does it dictate the salary that can be paid from a NIH research grant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH states it does not set salaries for staff on research mechanisms; local institutions determine pay rates. Use institutional salary policies when determining salaries to request on research grants rather than assuming NRSA levels automatically apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is an NIH executive pay cap
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is an upper limit, aka 'cap', which is currently $221,900 (NOT-OD-24-057).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salaries charged to NIH grants should not exceed the official NIH cap. Although an institution could theoretically place staff at the cap, this is not commonly done; institutional practices vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is acceptable to charge a person's current wage and benefits to a research grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the typical range of various staff salaries, the author has not seen problems from NIH’s perspective in paying the person’s current wage and benefits from a research mechanism grant (senior techs, postdocs, even those at/over cap in the author's experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When budgeting, charging an employee’s customary institutional salary (within policy and cap) to a research grant is generally acceptable. Expect institutional and sponsor-level variance; document institutional salary policies if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: NRSA stipends may not be supplemented from the research grant that supports the trainee’s training activities
rubrics_metrics.description: “No, it is not okay to supplement NRSA salaries off the research grant that pays for the training activities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementation (i.e., increasing the stipend provided by an NRSA with funds from the research grant that funds the trainee’s training activities) is disallowed. Be careful to avoid charging research grants to pay extra stipend for the same training-supported research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible compensation for part-time work unrelated to NRSA research (25% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception: an allowable 25% time compensation for the person working on a grant unrelated to the subject of the NRSA or other job. Quoted guidance: 'Under these conditions, the funds provided as compensation (salary, fringe benefits, and/or tuition remission) for services rendered ... are not considered stipend supplementation; they are allowable charges to Federal grants, including PHS research grants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation from research grants is allowable for limited part-time employment that is separate from the trainee’s full-time training activities and not for the same research that is part of the trainee’s planned training experience. Ensure the work is genuinely unrelated and limited in time (NIH references/NRSAs and supplementation policy should be consulted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate NRSA tuition coverage limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate student NRSAs can pay up to 60% (to a limit of $16,000 per year) of any tuition charged by the institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any tuition beyond the 60%/ $16,000 cap must be covered by the institution or PIs from discretionary (non-federal) funds; do not assume NIH will cover the remainder via research grant funds unless institution policy permits and it is allowable under the applicable grant terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: When budgeting use institutional operating salary levels for traditional R01 budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: If preparing a traditional budget R01 proposal, 'I would simply use the operating salary levels at my University for the postdoc position.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the institution’s standard salary scale when listing salaries on grant budgets. Do not substitute NRSA levels unless institutional policy or the specific funding mechanism requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: NRSA increases can sometimes justify requesting higher postdoc salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: If an institution pays postdocs less than NRSA scale, the NRSA increase could potentially be used to argue the pre-award folks into letting a PI ask for a higher salary on a grant application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NRSA levels can be leveraged internally to seek permission to request higher salaries on grants, but success depends on institutional HR/policy and pre-award offices. This is a possible avenue when local pay lags NRSA scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer perceptions about salary requests can affect funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers form a general impression and may comment if they think the PI is 'asking for too much money' which can have a detrimental effect on review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modular budgets and reviewer behavior vary, aligning requested salaries to institutional norms or NRSA levels (where appropriate) may reduce the risk of negative reviewer comments. Expect some subjectivity; be prepared to justify higher salary requests with institutional scales and explanations of role/experience.
